title: MYCIN — 1975 Clinical Therapeutics Publication
summary: In August 1975, Edward H. Shortliffe, Randall Davis, Stanton G. Axline, Bruce G. Buchanan, C. Cordell Green, and Stanley N. Cohen published a paper describing progress on MYCIN, an interactive computer program designed to advise physicians about selecting antimicrobial therapy for hospital patients with bacterial infections.
significance: A directly dated publication milestone documenting MYCIN as a functioning rule-based medical consultation system. LINEAiGE records this as a 1975 publication/documentation milestone, not as MYCIN's invention date, first implementation date, or universal system-birth date.

verification.note: The U.S. National Library of Medicine's PubMed record identifies the article, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, DOI, and publication month as August 1975. Stanford Medicine's later first-party retrospective identifies the MYCIN project as spanning 1972-1979 and Shortliffe's doctoral work as completed in 1976. This candidate uses only the publication milestone supported by the 1975 paper and does not infer a precise MYCIN creation date, first-ever status, geography, ancestry, influence, causality, or relationships.

sources.title: Computer-based consultations in clinical therapeutics: explanation and rule acquisition capabilities of the MYCIN system
sources.publisher: Computers and Biomedical Research / U.S. National Library of Medicine (PubMed)

sources.title: Stanford DBDS Seminar — Edward H. Shortliffe — 4 February 2021

candidateMeta.admissionReason: The 1975 peer-reviewed paper directly documents MYCIN and has stable bibliographic metadata at PubMed. The record can be retained as a dated publication milestone without converting that publication date into an unsupported system-birth claim.
candidateMeta.nextStep: Before canonical admission, reconcile this 1975 publication with the project's earlier 1972-1974 development history, Shortliffe's 1976 dissertation, and subsequent MYCIN evaluation publications. Keep publication, development, dissertation, and evaluation milestones distinct unless primary evidence supports consolidation.
